exercises.solutionExplanation:
The generator expression inside "

".join(...) formats each chunk dict into a two-line string -- a bracketed source label, then the chunk's text -- and joining those with "

" puts exactly one blank line between chunks, so multiple retrieved chunks stay visually distinct instead of running together. The outer return statement then wraps that already-assembled context string into the fixed instruction template, using an f-string to drop in both the context block and the original question. Running it on the two sample handbook chunks produces one clean, self-contained prompt string that an LLM call would receive as its entire input for this request -- with both retrieved facts clearly labeled by source, which is exactly what lets a well-behaved model produce an answer that can cite 'handbook.md#section-4' or '#section-7' specifically, rather than an unattributed claim.

assessments.prompt: A search feature runs an unfiltered ANN search for the top 5 nearest documents, then filters that list of 5 down to only documents the requesting user has permission to see. For a user who can only see a small fraction of the overall collection, what is the most likely observable problem with this design?
options: It will run noticeably slower than an equivalent brute-force search.
It will frequently return fewer than 5 results -- sometimes zero -- even when the user actually has plenty of permitted, relevant documents in the collection.
It will return documents the user isn't permitted to see, since the filter is applied too late to matter.
It will raise an exception when no permitted documents appear in the initial top 5.
assessments.explanation: This is post-filtering, and its specific, well-known failure mode is exactly this: filtering happens after the ANN step already committed to a fixed top-5, unfiltered candidate list, so if few or none of the user's permitted documents happen to be among the overall 5 closest matches, the final filtered result silently comes back with fewer than 5 items, or none at all, even though the user's permitted documents include perfectly relevant matches sitting further down the unfiltered ranking. Option A is wrong -- post-filtering is normally cheaper, not slower, than pre-filtering, precisely because it still benefits from the ANN index's speedup on the initial (unfiltered) search. Option C describes the opposite problem -- post-filtering, applied correctly, does remove documents the user can't see, it just does so too late to recover documents it should have found instead; it doesn't leak anything unpermitted here. Option D is wrong because the code in question (a simple list-comprehension filter) doesn't raise on an empty result -- it just silently returns an empty or short list, which is exactly what makes this bug easy to miss.

assessments.prompt: A vector database applies pre-filtering for a boolean metadata flag that happens to be true for 90% of the entire collection. What's the likely performance consequence?
options: Pre-filtering becomes faster than usual in this case, since fewer vectors technically need to be considered.

Pre-filtering degenerates toward directly scanning almost the entire collection, since most ANN index structures are built once over the whole collection and a low-selectivity filter barely narrows the candidate set down at all -- losing most of the speedup the ANN index was built to provide.
Pre-filtering will return incorrect results whenever a filter matches more than 50% of the collection.
Pre-filtering has no performance cost regardless of filter selectivity, since by construction it is always at least as fast as post-filtering.
assessments.explanation: The explanation is explicit that naive pre-filtering's speed depends on filter selectivity: it restricts to the matching subset first, then scans that subset directly (brute-force, not via the ANN index), which is cheap only when the filter rules out most of the collection. A filter that barely narrows anything down -- like a boolean flag true for 90% of documents -- means pre-filtering ends up directly scanning almost the whole collection, defeating the purpose of having built an ANN index in the first place. Option A gets the direction backwards for a high-selectivity-in-the-wrong-direction filter like this one. Option C invents a correctness threshold that doesn't exist -- pre-filtering remains correct regardless of selectivity, it just gets slower. Option D is false -- the explanation explicitly frames pre-filtering's cost as selectivity-dependent, not uniformly cheap.

assessments.prompt: Mature production vector databases often build metadata filtering directly into ANN traversal rather than choosing purely between naive pre-filtering and post-filtering. Which of the following describes one real approach to this, as covered in the explanation?
options: During HNSW's greedy graph walk, skip nodes that don't match the filter without terminating the search early, and continue exploring the graph past them.
Append the metadata value as an extra numeric dimension directly onto each embedding vector, turning the filter into an ordinary part of the distance calculation.
Run the same unfiltered ANN search twice, independently, and intersect the two resulting sets of candidates.
Convert the metadata filter into a query against a separate relational database and discard the vector index's results entirely.
assessments.explanation: The explanation describes exactly this as 'filtered graph traversal': check each candidate node's metadata against the filter as part of HNSW's normal greedy walk, skip non-matching nodes without stopping the search, and keep walking past them to continue exploring the graph -- integrating the filter into traversal itself rather than treating it as a separate before/after step. Option B describes a technique not mentioned anywhere in the explanation and would corrupt the geometry the distance calculation depends on. Option C would not reliably solve the problem post-filtering already has, since running the identical unfiltered search twice would just return the identical unfiltered top-k twice. Option D describes discarding the vector index's actual value entirely, which isn't a form of integrating filtering into ANN search at all.

assessments.prompt: In a RAG pipeline, why must the query be embedded, at request time, using the exact same embedding model that was used to embed and index the source document chunks ahead of time?
options: It's a stylistic convention rather than a hard requirement -- any reasonably capable modern embedding model would work interchangeably with any other.

Different embedding models produce independent, uncalibrated vector spaces, so comparing a query vector from one model against document vectors from another would yield similarity scores with no real meaning, silently corrupting retrieval without raising any error.
Using a different model only actually matters if the two models happen to produce vectors of different dimensionality.
The embedding model choice only affects the quality of the LLM's generated answer, not the retrieval step that happens before it.
assessments.explanation: This is the 'don't mix embedding model versions' rule from the very first concept in this subject, explicitly resurfacing here as a hard requirement for RAG: since two embedding models carve out unrelated, uncalibrated vector spaces, a similarity score computed between a query vector from one model and document vectors from another doesn't correspond to any real relationship -- it will still return some number, with no error or warning, but that number is meaningless, silently producing bad or irrelevant retrieval. Option A is precisely the mistake this rule exists to prevent. Option C is wrong -- matching dimensionality is coincidental and doesn't fix the underlying incompatibility between two independently-trained vector spaces. Option D is wrong because this is fundamentally a retrieval-stage problem -- the wrong or irrelevant chunks get retrieved before generation ever happens, which is exactly the kind of retrieval bug the explanation warns gets mistaken for a generation failure.

assessments.prompt: A RAG-powered support chatbot occasionally gives a confident, plausible-sounding, but factually wrong answer, and a teammate suggests the fix is to try a different LLM or add stricter prompt instructions. Explain why you'd want to investigate retrieval first, and what specifically you'd check.
assessments.modelAnswer: Before assuming the generation step is at fault, it's worth remembering that the LLM has no way to know whether the context it was handed is actually relevant -- it's simply given whatever text the retrieval step produced and asked to answer using it, and a capable model will confidently synthesize a plausible-sounding answer from irrelevant or wrong context just as readily as from good context, which is exactly why a retrieval failure and a genuine generation failure can look identical from the outside: a confident, wrong answer either way. In practice, a large share of real RAG failures turn out to be retrieval bugs rather than generation bugs, and several specific, checkable things from earlier in this subject cause exactly this symptom: the query might have been embedded with a different model version than the one used to build the index (producing similarity scores that are silently meaningless rather than simply low), the ANN index's recall might be tuned too low for how precisely this use case needs to retrieve (missing the one chunk that actually contains the correct answer), or a metadata filtering bug might be leaking in irrelevant or wrong-scope content instead of the right chunks. The concrete first step is to log and inspect exactly what chunks were retrieved for the specific failing query -- if the retrieved context genuinely doesn't contain the information needed to answer correctly, that's conclusive: the model did about as well as it could with what it was given, and the fix belongs in retrieval (re-checking embedding model consistency, raising recall, auditing filters), not in swapping models or tightening prompt wording, which would be treating the symptom rather than the actual upstream cause.
